The company, the platform, the tenant teams and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the platform engineer responsible for cost at Thistledown Media, a fictional publisher. The shared Kubernetes platform's bill is 40% over budget this quarter. Finance wants a plan in three weekly reviews.
handover: OpenCost is installed; nobody reads it. Most Deployments request about three times the CPU and memory they use.
Node count is fixed at 60 large nodes; there is no cluster autoscaler.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each cost review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

sizePrompt.title: Requests three times usage
sizePrompt.context: Cutting requests frees nodes; cutting too far causes throttling and OOM kills.

choices.label: Set requests from each workload's 95th-percentile usage plus headroom, using VPA in recommendation mode, staging first, then production team by team
choices.feedback: Measured usage with headroom, staged, frees capacity without starving workloads.

choices.label: Right-size staging only this quarter
choices.feedback: Safe, but production is where most of the idle cost is.

choices.label: Cut every request by 60% across the cluster this week
choices.feedback: A flat cut ignores which workloads are tight: the month-end jobs are starved.

showPrompt.title: Who pays for what?
showPrompt.context: OpenCost can allocate by namespace and label; teams never see their costs.

choices.label: Monthly showback per team from OpenCost by namespace and team label, including idle cost of what each team requests

effects.log: Each team gets its costs, idle included.

choices.feedback: Allocation by namespace and label shows each team the cost of what it requests, which is what changes behavior.

choices.label: Keep all costs on the platform's budget and publish a cluster total
choices.feedback: Visible, but no team sees what its own requests cost.

choices.label: Split the bill evenly across the 20 teams
choices.feedback: The smallest teams pay for the biggest; nobody has a reason to request less.

scalePrompt.title: 60 fixed nodes for a spiky load
scalePrompt.context: Usage is low most of the month and triples at month-end.

choices.label: Add a cluster autoscaler with a 30 to 80 node range, HPAs on the spiky services, and priority classes so customer-facing workloads win over batch

effects.log: The cluster scales with demand; priorities protect customer-facing work.

choices.feedback: Nodes follow demand; priority classes decide who waits when capacity is short.

choices.label: Drop to 45 fixed nodes
choices.feedback: Cheaper most of the month, tight at month-end.

choices.label: Cap the cluster at 30 nodes with no autoscaler

effects.log: The cluster is capped at 30 nodes.

choices.feedback: Month-end needs more than 30 nodes; customer-facing Pods sit Pending with the batch jobs.

scoring.modelReasoning: Kubernetes cost follows requests, not usage: requests three times usage leave nodes idle. Right-size from measured usage percentiles with headroom, staged (VPA recommendations help), rather than flat cuts. OpenCost allocates cost by namespace and label, so showback per team, idle included, makes the cost of requests visible. Scale capacity with demand (cluster autoscaler, HPA), and use priority classes so critical workloads win when capacity is short.
